relations.note: Ọ̀rànmíyàn is Ajaka’s father in the principal Oyo royal genealogy.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 147–148

relations.note: Ọ̀rànmíyàn leaves Ajaka as regent; Ajaka is installed during his prolonged absence.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 147–148

relations.note: Ṣàngó is Ajaka’s younger brother, or half-brother in some later accounts.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 148–154

relations.note: Ṣàngó replaces the deposed Ajaka; Ajaka returns after Ṣàngó’s death.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 148–154

relations.note: Bahian traditions variously describe Dadá Ajaká as Xangô’s elder brother or sister.
relations.source: Querino and Verger traditions summarized by Castillo

relations.note: One Bahian variant identifies Dadá Ajaká as Xangô’s mother.
Some Bahian traditions treat Dadá Ajaká as a quality or form of Xangô.
relations.source: Querino, Verger, and later Bahian fieldwork

relations.note: Ajaka descends dynastically from Oduduwa through Ọ̀rànmíyàn; the intervening generations vary.
relations.source: Johnson and later Yoruba royal genealogies

relations.note: Aganju is Ajaka’s son and successor in the principal Oyo genealogy.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 154–155

relations.note: Elenre serves Ajaka as one of his named magical specialists.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 152–154

relations.note: Ajaka orders Elenre’s execution; the resulting wonder-tale produces Odo Elenre.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 152–154

relations.note: Egbeji serves Ajaka and disappears into heaven by climbing a suspended cord.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 152–154

relations.note: Ijaehin appears within Ajaka’s execution narrative but has no isolated direct exchange with him.
relations.source: Johnson, History of the Yorubas, pp. 152–154
